catalog_locator: sec. 2 'Phonology', 2.2 'Tones', p. 34 (journal pagination; page header '34 Ekaterina Aplonova and Victoria Pozdniakova' precedes the section, '35' precedes 2.3 'Phonotactics'); parallel statement in Aplonova 2025 PhD (INALCO, HAL tel-05356818) sec. 2.1.2 'Tones', p. 31
catalog_quote: 2.2. Tones Ginyanga has two phonological tones: high and low. A tone-bearing unit contains only one vowel. Consider examples (15)-(16) where segmentally identical words with different tones have different lexical meanings. (15) wù ‘see!’ (imperative) – wú ‘die!’ (imperative) (16) nàrɩ̀ ‘spider’ – nárɩ́ ‘ox’ A nasal /n/ can bear tones. See, for instance, that ń- is a high-toned 1sg Imperfective prefix (17) (§3.3.2) in opposition to ǹ-, a low-toned cl6 prefix (18) (§3.1), while [ŋ̀], a variant of /n/ that might be the result of a contraction, is a high-toned 1sg Future prefix (19) (§3.3.3). ... Tones are also used to distinguish between the basic aspectual opposition of Imperfective vs. Perfective. The Imperfective prefix has a high tone (20), while the first vowel of the Perfective has a low tone and the second one has a high tone (21).
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Ginyanga is described as a two-tone (H, L) language with the vowel (and syllabic nasal) as tone-bearing unit; tone is lexically and grammatically contrastive. The source's phonology section (inventory, tones, phonotactics) makes no statement at all about word stress or accent, and no other accessible description does either.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. (On tone: noun-prefix tone is polar to the stem-initial tone with some exceptions such as ótú 'heart', per Pozdniakova & Aplonova 2024.)
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns lexical/grammatical tone at word level; prosody of larger units explicitly left unanalysed in Aplonova 2025 PhD. No stress domain is described.
new_statements.identity_note: All accessed sources describe Ginyanga as spoken in Agbandi (and Diguina), Prefecture of Blitta, central Togo (fieldwork 2019-2024); same language as Glottolog giny1241 / ISO ayg (autonym anyanga for the people; Logossou 2009 uses 'anyanga' for the language). Gichode (gich1236) is mentioned as a closely related language/dialect but is not the object of description.
